"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5504: a diffuse readout with almost no token-level signal.

What the component is: one rank-one piece of the MLP down projection. It reads the MLP's
hidden units, led by hidden unit 5504 (0.43 of its 0.84-norm input direction, the rest spread
over many units), and writes a small direction into the residual stream. Its activation is
mostly small noise (std 0.33, mean 0.02), with rare large negative spikes (down to about
-8) on code and technical text, and rare positive spikes on prose and maths.

What this program does: predicts a small value from the kind of the current token alone.
Word-like tokens lean slightly positive, digits more so, punctuation and whitespace slightly
negative. The means are fit on about 2,000 training rows (1M tokens). The program keeps no
state and reads only the newest token.

Why it is this simple: no token-level or context-level feature we tried explains much of the
activation. A lookup on the exact current token reaches about 3% out of sample (a table of
150k token ids, which has no concept behind it, so it is not used here), and these coarse
kinds about 0.6-0.7%. Eval: variance explained 0.5%, r 0.07; e2e KL is the same as switching
the component off. The spikes depend on context that the program cannot see.
"""

import re

READS = ()

# Mean activation for each kind of current token, fit on training rows.
KIND_MEAN = {"word": 0.038, "digit": 0.055, "punct": -0.021, "space": -0.013, "other": 0.068}


def kind(text):
    """The coarse kind of one token, from its text decoded alone."""
    if text.strip() == "":
        return "space"
    if "�" in text or re.search(r"[　-鿿가-힯]", text):
        return "other"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?\d+", text):
        return "digit"
    if re.fullmatch(r"\s?[^\w\s]+", text):
        return "punct"
    return "word"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """This component's activation at the newest token, from that token's kind."""
    return carry, KIND_MEAN[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5505.

What it is: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its input direction V is
almost entirely MLP hidden unit 5505 of layer 15, so its activation is that unit's value
(gated: silu(gate) * up) scaled by the output norm. Its output, when negative, pushes the
next-token distribution toward words like "further", "subdivide", "multiple" and "again".

What this program does: it predicts a small negative value on the words that talk about
splitting something into kinds, types, groups or subcategories (the discourse of
classification: "divided into two types", "is further classified as", "comprises",
"subgroups"), and a small baseline everywhere else. Its predictions are only the average
level of the activation on those words; it captures the sign and rough size of the
dip, not the large, context-dependent spikes.

What it misses: most of the variance. Token identity explains only about 2% of the
activation's variance out of sample, and this word list about 0.1%. The large negative
spikes (down to -30) depend on context the program does not model.
"""

READS = ()

# Words about dividing a whole into kinds, types, groups or subcategories.
SUBDIVIDE = frozenset(
    {
        "type", "types", "kind", "kinds", "category", "categories", "class", "classes",
        "classified", "classification", "group", "groups", "subgroup", "subgroups",
        "subset", "subsets", "section", "sections", "subsection", "subsections",
        "part", "parts", "divided", "divide", "divides", "dividing", "split",
        "comprise", "comprises", "comprising", "consist", "consists", "consisting",
        "further", "subdivision", "subdivisions", "subdivided", "subdivide", "sub",
        "two", "into", "variety", "varieties", "subtype", "subtypes",
    }
)

BASELINE = 0.026  # the component's average activation
SUBDIVIDE_VALUE = -0.16  # its average activation on those words


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Predict the activation at the newest token from that token's word alone."""
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    value = SUBDIVIDE_VALUE if word in SUBDIVIDE else BASELINE
    return carry, float(value)

"""Colon detector for layer 15's MLP down-projection, component 5506.

What it does: this component sits silent on nearly every token and goes negative on
a colon. A token that contains a colon used as punctuation (":", ":\\n", '":', "):",
"：", " :", "**:", ...) gets a negative value. Its size depends on how many colons
came earlier in the same document: the first colon is the most negative (-3.6), the
second is -2.6, and later ones are -1.8, so routine colons (lists, "Label: value"
lines after the first one) hit less hard. Two cases are special: "::" (C++/Rust
scope) gives 0, and "://" (URLs) gives a weak -0.6. Every other token predicts 0.

Why: the sign and location come from the colon itself; the fall-off with earlier
colons is the one context effect that a simple count captures. Most of the remaining
variance is small, token-to-token noise with no simple rule behind it.
"""

READS = ()

COLON_CHARS = (":", "：", "∶")


def _colon_value(token, seen):
    if not any(ch in token for ch in COLON_CHARS):
        return 0.0
    if "::" in token:
        return 0.0
    if "://" in token:
        return -0.6
    if seen == 0:
        return -3.6
    if seen == 1:
        return -2.6
    return -1.8


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    seen = 0
    if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc:
        seen = carry[1]
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    value = _colon_value(token, seen)
    if value != 0.0 and "::" not in token:
        seen += 1
    return (doc, seen), value

"""p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5507, a near-silent MLP feature.

What it is: a rank-one readout of layer 15's MLP hidden units. Its activation is a
linear function of those units, and most of it is spread thinly over thousands of
units; MLP unit 5507 alone carries about a fifth of its variance. Overall it is a
diffuse function of the residual stream (a linear map of the layer's normalized input
explains about a third of it on held-out tokens). It has no clear token, bigram or
word-class trigger, and its write direction does not point at a readable set of
next tokens. The component is nearly silent in the model (it fires on no token above
the harvest threshold).

What this program captures: only a weak drift with position in the document. Right
after a document starts the activation leans slightly positive, and deep into a
document it leans slightly negative. Everything else is predicted as 0. This explains
a fraction of a percent of the variance; the rest is not captured.
"""

import math

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or doc != carry[0]:
        start = t  # a new document begins at this token
    else:
        start = carry[1]
    pos = t - start  # position within the current document
    if pos == 0:
        value = 0.0
    else:
        value = 0.0437 - 0.00983 * math.log2(pos)
    return (doc, start), value

"""Activation of component 5508 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj (Qwen3-1.7B).

What the component does: it reads one direction of the layer-15 MLP hidden state
(mostly the hidden unit 5508, plus a diffuse spread over the rest) and writes it back into
the residual stream. Its activation is spread out and noise-like, and most of it is not
explained by the current token. Its strongest negative values are on the decimal point of a
number, as in "3.14", "Version 2.0" or "PM2.5". A period that is not inside a number
(a sentence end) is mildly positive.

This program predicts only those rules, from the current token and the one before it:
  - a period right after a digit (a decimal point): -0.7
  - any other period: +0.15
  - every other token: 0.06, the component's mean activation

Qwen splits numbers into single digits, so "the previous token is a digit" means
"the period is inside a number". The previous token only counts within the same document.
"""

READS = ()

BASE = 0.06
DECIMAL_POINT = -0.7
OTHER_PERIOD = 0.15


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if tok != ".":
        return carry, BASE
    same_doc = len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip() if same_doc else ""
    return carry, DECIMAL_POINT if prev.isdigit() else OTHER_PERIOD

"""Layer 15, MLP hidden unit 5509 of Qwen3-1.7B (the component's activation is this one unit's
SwiGLU value, silu(gate) * up, scaled by about 0.77).

The unit is diffuse: no word or document type predicts it well. What it does respond to is a
purpose or means in the text. Its clearest high values are on:
  - "to" after a word for a method or use: "used to", "way to", "approach to", "method to",
    "alternative to", "equivalent to", "proportional to", "corresponding to";
  - verbs of achieving, obtaining or producing a result, such as "achieve", "obtain",
    "represent", "estimate", "generate", "determine", "calculate", and the adjective "desired";
  - more weakly, the everyday verbs of getting or making a thing: "get", "create", "find", "give".
Everywhere else it sits near a small negative baseline. This program predicts those classes.
"""

from functools import lru_cache

import wordnet

READS = ()

BASELINE = -0.09
"""The typical value of every other token."""

MEANS_WORDS = frozenset({
    "way", "ways", "method", "methods", "approach", "approaches", "technique", "techniques",
    "alternative", "alternatives", "strategy", "tool", "tools", "means", "used", "use",
    "utilized", "employed", "equivalent", "proportional", "corresponding", "adapted", "suited",
})
"""Words after which "to" opens a means, method or correspondence."""

RESULT_VERBS = frozenset({
    "achieve", "accomplish", "attain", "obtain", "produce", "generate", "yield", "derive",
    "estimate", "calculate", "compute", "determine", "simulate", "approximate", "quantify",
    "represent", "reconstruct", "recover", "retrieve", "implement", "construct", "capture",
    "detect", "extract", "desire",
})
"""Verbs (base forms) of achieving, obtaining, producing or working out a result."""

GETTING_VERBS = frozenset({"get", "create", "find", "give", "provide", "perform", "reach", "solve"})
"""Everyday verbs of getting or making something: weaker."""


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def base_form(word):
    """The verb's base form, through WordNet ("achieves" -> "achieve")."""
    forms = wordnet.base_forms(word)
    return forms[0] if forms else word


def verb_class(word):
    """'result', 'getting' or None for a lowercase word."""
    if not word.isalpha():
        return None
    base = base_form(word)
    if base in RESULT_VERBS:
        return "result"
    if base in GETTING_VERBS:
        return "getting"
    return None


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    after_to = before == "to"
    if word == "to":
        return carry, 1.5 if before in MEANS_WORDS else 0.1
    kind = verb_class(word)
    if kind == "result":
        return carry, 1.4 if after_to else 0.5
    if kind == "getting":
        return carry, 1.0 if after_to else 0.3
    return carry, BASELINE

"""Layer 15 MLP neuron 5510 (component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5510).

What it is: the component's read vector loads mainly on MLP hidden unit 5510
(about half of its energy), so its activation largely follows that unit's value.
Its write direction promotes words of sequence and direction ("then", "然后",
"向外" outward, "流向" flow toward, "转移到" transfer to, "扩散" spread).

What this program does: it predicts a small positive value on sequence words
("then", "whence", Japanese "から" from) and a small negative value on code and
markup tokens, and 0 elsewhere. Most of the neuron's variance is a diffuse,
context-dependent spread that no token or position rule captures, so this
program explains very little of it. It is kept short on purpose.
"""

READS = ()

# Words that start a next step or source in a path or sequence ("from there, then ...").
SEQUENCE_WORDS = {"then", "whence", "然后", "然后再", "后", "後", "から", "からの", "出发"}
# Markup, code and chat-template tokens, where the neuron tends to sit slightly below zero.
CODE_WORDS = {"also", "until", "using", "bash", "command", "//", ".md", "/src", "=", "#",
              "</tool_response>", "</tool_call>", "<|im_start|>", "<|im_end|>", "user", "assistant"}

SEQUENCE_VALUE = 0.4
CODE_VALUE = -0.08


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in SEQUENCE_WORDS:
        value = SEQUENCE_VALUE
    elif word in CODE_WORDS:
        value = CODE_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, float(value)

"""Predict the small average activation of MLP-output unit 5511 in layer 15, by kind of token.

This component is almost noise: its activation has standard deviation 0.3 around a mean of
0.02, and nothing in the token text explains much of it (token identity explains about 2%).
What little structure there is: it is exactly zero at the first token of each document (the
model has no context there), it is slightly higher on punctuation that follows a space, and
close to zero on newlines and on words that follow a space.
"""

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Average activation for each kind of token, measured on training text.
NEWLINE = 0.005
SPACE_WORD = 0.008
SPACE_PUNCT = 0.056
OTHER = 0.03


def kind_value(text):
    """Average activation for a token, from its text alone."""
    if "\n" in text:
        return NEWLINE
    if text[:1] == " " and text[1:2].isalpha():
        return SPACE_WORD
    if text[:1] == " " and text[1:2] and not text[1:2].isalnum():
        return SPACE_PUNCT
    return OTHER


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    first = len(prefix.token_ids) == 1 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    if first:
        return carry, 0.0
    return carry, kind_value(prefix.token_strings[-1])

"""Baseline program for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5512.

What the component is: a single rank-one readout of layer 15's MLP hidden state. Its input
direction V_c is dominated by hidden unit 5512 (weight 0.46 of its total norm 0.80), with
many small weights on other hidden units; its output norm is 0.94. Its activation is
roughly Gaussian around 0.04 with std 0.29, and it is almost never a large part of the
residual stream (RMS 0.5% of the site's output).

What was found: no readable rule predicts it. Token identity explains about 0.5% of its
variance (held out), the previous token about 0%, character class of the token and its
predecessor about 0.3%, and copying (a token seen earlier in the document) nothing at all.
Hidden unit 5512 itself is not token-driven either. The only clean regularity is at the
first token of each document, where the activation is ~0 (it is 0.004 on average there, and
0.046 elsewhere).

So this program predicts the component's mean value everywhere, and 0 at the first token of
each document. It is a baseline, not an explanation of the component's variance.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0454
"""The component's mean activation over training positions."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    """Predict the mean activation, except 0 at a document's first token."""
    t = prefix.position
    first_of_document = t == 0 or prefix.document_ids[t] != prefix.document_ids[t - 1]
    return carry, 0.0 if first_of_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5513: a constant prediction.

What the component does: its activation is (MLP hidden vector . V_c) * ||U_c||. Almost all of it
comes from one hidden unit of layer 15's MLP (unit 5513, weight 0.22) and, with a negative sign,
unit 2426. Those units depend on the whole context in a way that no token-level rule we tested
captures: token identity, the previous token, part of speech of the token or the previous token,
position in the document, and the document's overall type all explain about 0-2% of the variance
out of sample.

So this program does not try to track the component's ups and downs. It predicts the component's
average value over text, about +0.014 at every position. That is the best a readable rule gets
here: its variance explained is about zero, and it leaves the model's next-token predictions
essentially as switched off, since the component's own effect is tiny.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0143


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The component's activation at this position: its mean over text."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Colon detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 5514.

What it responds to: the colon that ends a label and introduces its content,
such as "Error reading file:", "Test Suites:", "Downloaded from central:" or
"Posted at:", plus a full-width "：" and colon-final tokens (":\n\n", '":', "?:").
Its activation is about 4 on average there. It is strongest at the first colon
of a document (about 6) and weaker for each later colon in the same document
(about 3 after many): value = 6.3 - 1.27 * log(1 + colons_before_in_document).
Indentation (about 0.4) and " =" (about 1.4) give a weaker positive value;
everything else is about 0. The rule explains about 15% of the variance; a
full per-token table adds only a few points more.
"""

import math
import re

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        colons_before = 0  # a new document starts here
    else:
        colons_before = carry[1]
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    core = tok.rstrip(" \n\t\\*")
    if core.endswith((":", "：")):
        value = 6.3 - 1.27 * math.log1p(colons_before)
        colons_before += 1
    elif re.fullmatch(r"\n?[ \t]+", tok):
        value = 0.4  # indentation
    elif tok == " =":
        value = 1.4
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (doc, colons_before), float(value)

"""Layer 15, MLP down_proj, component 5515: a near-constant predictor.

What the component reads: about half of its input direction's energy sits on one
MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (unit 5515), so its activation is largely that unit's
value times the component's output norm, plus a diffuse remainder. The unit is a
signed, context-dependent signal. Its value at a token is not set by the token's
identity, the next token, the token pair, its position in the document, whether the
token repeats an earlier one, or simple character classes (script, digits,
punctuation, code symbols). Checked on about 2 million tokens, none of these explains
more than a fraction of a percent of its variance.

What this program does: it predicts the component's average value (0.037) at every
token, except 0 at the first token of a document or row, where the component is
silent. This captures the mean level only, not the token-to-token variation.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.037  # the component's average value over all tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first_in_document = prefix.position == 0 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    value = 0.0 if first_in_document else MEAN_ACTIVATION
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 5516, as a position-in-document baseline.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of layers.15.mlp.down_proj whose read
direction is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 5516 of layer 15 (about 44% of its
squared weight). Its activation is a linear readout of that unit plus a diffuse
remainder over thousands of other units. The unit is polysemantic: its strongest
contexts share no single word, script, or topic, and its logit-lens output is a
scatter of unrelated sub-word fragments. Switching the component off changes the
model's output by almost nothing (KL about 2e-6 nats per position).

What this program does: it does not read the unit. It predicts only the drift of
the component's typical value with position inside a document: about zero on the
first token, a small negative value on the second, and a slowly growing negative
mean for later positions. Document position is counted from the last document
boundary, as the model resets its positions there.

This is a weak predictor (about 0.4% of activation variance on training rows). It
is kept because it is short and it is the only readable regularity found. A token
table or the neuron's own value would explain far more, but neither is a concept.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def expected(pos: int) -> float:
    """Typical activation at document position `pos` (0 = first token)."""
    if pos == 0:
        return 0.0
    if pos == 1:
        return -0.12
    if pos < 16:
        return 0.0
    if pos < 64:
        return -0.02
    if pos < 256:
        return -0.05
    return -0.07


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    return (doc, pos), float(expected(pos))

"""Predicts the component's activation from position in the document.

The component's activation is a diffuse readout of the MLP hidden state. The
only consistent pattern found is at a document's second token (position 1),
where it sits near -0.13 on average, and it is near zero elsewhere. Everything
else is predicted as 0. Position resets at each new document in a packed row.
"""

READS = ()

SECOND_TOKEN_MEAN = -0.134


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        n = 0
    else:
        n = carry[1] + 1
    value = SECOND_TOKEN_MEAN if n == 1 else 0.0
    return (doc, n), value

"""Contrast-marker detector for one MLP down-projection component (layer 15).

What it does: it fires on the word that turns an argument around: the "but" of
"..., but I guess", "However, ...", "Wait, ..." or "Hmm, but ...". These are
clause-initial contrastive connectives (or self-correction cues such as "Wait"
and "Wait, no"), in English and a few other languages. Each has a strength that
follows how strongly the component fires on it. The component also keeps firing
a little on the punctuation or word right after such a connective ("However,"),
so the token after one gets a fraction of its strength. Everywhere else it
predicts 0: on ordinary text its activation is small and diffuse, which a short
list cannot capture.
"""

READS = ()

# Contrastive connectives and self-correction cues, with typical activation.
CONTRAST = {
    "however": 5.0,
    "but": 4.4,
    "但是": 3.6,
    "aber": 3.6,
    "但": 2.0,
    "wait": 4.0,
    "unfortunately": 2.4,
    "hmm": 2.0,
    "though": 2.2,
    "although": 1.6,
    "yet": 1.2,
}
# "no" right after "Wait" (as in "Wait, no") is a strong self-correction.
WAIT_NO = 8.0
# Share of a connective's strength that the next token carries.
FOLLOW = 0.4


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if len(prefix.token_strings) > 1 else ""
    if word == "no" and prev == "wait":
        return carry, WAIT_NO
    if word in CONTRAST:
        return carry, CONTRAST[word]
    if prev in CONTRAST:
        return carry, FOLLOW * CONTRAST[prev]
    return carry, 0.0

"""Component layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5519, as a position-in-document offset.

What the component is: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its input
direction is almost entirely MLP hidden unit 5519 of that layer (about half of its input
energy), so its activation is roughly 0.55 times that unit's value, silu(gate) * up. That
unit is a dense feature of the residual stream: its value varies from token to token in
ways that token identity, the previous or next token, simple lexical or citation patterns,
and the model's own next-token predictions do not capture (held-out R^2 below 0.01 for each).

What this program does: it predicts the one regularity found. Near the start of a document
the activation is negative on average (about -0.2 at positions 1-5, fading to about -0.1 by
position 15), and it is more spread out there. The program predicts that mean by position
within the document, and 0 everywhere else. That explains only about half a percent of the
variance; it is a small effect, not a description of what the component computes.
"""

READS = ()


def mean_by_position(pos):
    """Mean activation of the component at `pos` tokens into its document."""
    if 1 <= pos <= 5:
        return -0.23
    if 6 <= pos <= 8:
        return -0.14
    if 9 <= pos <= 15:
        return -0.09
    return 0.0


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # Position within the current document: restarts where the document label changes.
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        pos = 0
    else:
        pos = carry[1] + 1
    return (doc, pos), mean_by_position(pos)

"""Decimal-point detector (layer 15 MLP, component 5520).

What it does: this component fires on the "." that follows a number, i.e. the
decimal point in "3.14", "$3.", "version 2.1", "finished in 0.5 s". The model
is about to read the digits after the point, and this component writes a
large positive value there. Other number punctuation (commas and colons between
digits) gives a smaller value. A "." after a number that starts a line
("1. Start with...", list numbering) or after a four-digit year ("in 2019.")
is usually a sentence or list end, so it gets a much smaller value.

Everything else is predicted as 0. The component's activation on ordinary
tokens is a diffuse, token-independent spread that this program does not model.
"""

READS = ()

DIGITS = set("0123456789")

DECIMAL_DOT = 3.4  # "." after a number, typical
DOLLAR_DOT = 7.4  # "$3." : price with a decimal point
LINE_START_DOT = 0.7  # "1." at the start of a line: list numbering
YEAR_DOT = 0.6  # "2019." : four digits, usually a sentence end
COMMA = 0.7  # "1,043": thousands separator
COLON = 1.2  # "20:00": time


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    cur = toks[-1]
    value = 0.0

What it does: the component is strongly negative on a colon (":") or a colon-like
separator that introduces a label's value or a message, e.g. "Posts: 56", "Test Suites:",
"Got: %v", "Article 7.1"-style decimal points and assignment signs ("=", " =") in code
and maths. It is near zero on almost every other token. The effect is stronger near the
start of a document, where the same separators are roughly 1.8x as negative as late in a
long document.

What the program predicts: a signed activation.
  - colon-like token         -> about -4.6   (times the position boost)
  - "=" or " =" sign         -> about -2.3   (times the position boost)
  - "." directly after a digit (decimal point, "1.5") -> about -1.8 (times the boost)
  - anything else            -> 0
  - position boost: 1 + 0.9 * exp(-p / 40), where p is the token's position in its document.

The program keeps only a document-start marker in its carry, so it resets at each new
document in a packed row, as the model does.
"""

import math

READS = ()

# Colon-like separators, as tokens: ":", full-width "：", and colon fused with a newline,
# quote, bracket or "=" ("\":", "):", ":\n", ":=").
COLON_TOKENS = {":", "：", ":\n", ":\n\n", ":\\", '":', "):", " :", " :=", ":="}
EQUALS_TOKENS = {"=", " ="}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")

COLON_VALUE = -4.6
EQUALS_VALUE = -2.3
DECIMAL_POINT_VALUE = -1.8


def position_boost(p):
    """Separators are more negative near the start of a document: 1.9x at p=0, 1.0x late."""
    return 1 + 0.9 * math.exp(-p / 40)


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # carry: (document label, index of that document's first token) for the newest token.
    n = len(prefix.token_ids)
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    start = carry[1] if carry and carry[0] == doc else n - 1
    p = n - 1 - start

    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if n > 1 else ""
    if tok in COLON_TOKENS:
        value = COLON_VALUE
    elif tok in EQUALS_TOKENS:
        value = EQUALS_VALUE
    elif tok == "." and prev.strip()[-1:] in DIGITS:
        value = DECIMAL_POINT_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (doc, start), value * position_boost(p)

to 20. The same period after a number that starts a line (numbered-list "3." or an
identifier like "pkg__1.") is weak. Every other token sits near a small negative
baseline, the mean of its activation there.

The program is three rules:
  1. a "." right after a digit, mid-line            -> 3.1
  2. a "." right after a digit that starts a line   -> 0.6
  3. every other token                              -> -0.1

Rule 1 is the component's strongest response and the one the harvest picks out. Most of
the component's variance is a broad, token-level spread over ordinary tokens that no short
rule captures; a per-token table would add only a few points of variance explained and is
not readable.
"""

READS = ()

MID_NUMBER = 3.1  # a decimal point inside a line of text
LINE_START_NUMBER = 0.6  # a numbered-list "3." at the start of a line
BASELINE = -0.1  # every other token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    toks = prefix.token_strings
    t = len(toks) - 1
    value = BASELINE
    same_doc = t >= 1 and prefix.document_ids[t - 1] == prefix.document_ids[t]
    if same_doc and toks[t] == "." and toks[t - 1].isdigit():
        starts_line = t >= 2 and "\n" in toks[t - 2]
        value = LINE_START_NUMBER if starts_line else MID_NUMBER
    return carry, value
